name: Mount Kailash
scope: A pyramidal peak (6,638 m) in the Gangdise range of far-western Tibet, near the China–India–Nepal tripoint. T1: of all the great Himalayan-region summits, this is the one NO ONE has ever climbed — climbing is forbidden out of reverence (invert the wonder: the hook is that far smaller peaks are summited daily; the answer is that Kailash stands untrodden). T2: it is held sacred at once by FOUR faiths — Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and the older Bon (answer is 'four'; distractors are 'one/two/three' plus rival named mountains). T3: pilgrims don't go up but AROUND — a ~52 km circuit at the base, the kora/parikrama, walked clockwise by most and counter-clockwise by the Bon. T4: the headwaters of four of Asia's great rivers — the Indus, the Sutlej, the Brahmaputra (Yarlung Tsangpo), and the Karnali (a Ganges feeder) — all rise in the region around this one mountain. T5: at its foot lie twin lakes — freshwater Manasarovar, among the highest freshwater lakes on Earth (~4,590 m), beside the saltier Rakshastal: a fresh lake and a salt lake side by side. Deep: spread across ~12 rungs (add the names Kangrinboqe/Gang Rinpoche, the 21,778 ft height as a hook, Reinhold Messner reportedly declining the climb, the Gangdise/Kailash range).
source: Grokipedia/Mount_Kailash attempted first (HTTP 403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash — height 6,638 m, never summited/climbing prohibited, sacred to Hinduism/Buddhism/Jainism/Bon, ~53 km circumambulation, Indus/Sutlej/Brahmaputra/Karnali rise within ~60 km, Lake Manasarovar (~320 km2, among highest freshwater lakes) + Rakshastal.
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER, respectful, never advertising or dismissing a faith — doctrine is the theology bank's; here the answer is always a fact about the MOUNTAIN and its landscape. Accuracy rail: the four rivers rise in the REGION AROUND Kailash, not literally from the summit (say 'nearby'/'in the region'), and give Manasarovar as 'among the highest' freshwater lakes, not a bare 'the highest' (that superlative is contested). Dinner-test payoff: the four-rivers rung — one mountain feeds the Indus, Brahmaputra, Sutlej, and a branch of the Ganges. vision_mandated: the reverence that keeps it unclimbed is the heart — honor it on its own terms, no smug secular dismissal.

name: The Ganges: from Gaumukh to the ghats of Varanasi
scope: The course of the Ganga from ice to ghats. T1: the river is born at GAUMUKH ('cow's mouth'), the icy snout of the Gangotri Glacier in the Uttarakhand Himalaya (~4,000 m) — invert the wonder: the vast holy river of the plains starts as meltwater dripping from one glacier's toe. T2: it is not yet called the Ganga until DEVPRAYAG, where the Bhagirathi headstream meets the green Alaknanda and the two become one river. T3: at Varanasi (Kashi/Benares), one of the world's oldest continuously lived-in cities, the river bends in a great CRESCENT and 84 stone ghats step down the west bank — all facing east across the water toward the sunrise. T4: two of those ghats, Manikarnika and Harishchandra, are cremation ghats where fires burn day and night (the NAMED place, not a doctrine, is the answer). T5: ~2,500 km on, the Ganges joins the Brahmaputra and empties through the world's LARGEST river delta, the Sundarbans, into the Bay of Bengal. Deep: ~12 rungs (add the Triveni Sangam at Prayagraj as a mid-course rung, the Dashashwamedh evening aarti, the Marathas rebuilding the ghats in the 1700s).
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges (Gaumukh/Gangotri Glacier source at ~4,356 m, Bhagirathi+Alaknanda form the Ganga at Devprayag, ~2,525 km, Ganges–Brahmaputra delta ~64,000 km2 = world's largest) and /Varanasi + /Ghats_in_Varanasi (west-bank crescent, 84 official ghats, Manikarnika & Harishchandra cremation ghats, Dashashwamedh aarti, most ghats rebuilt under 18th-c Maratha patronage).
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER told with respect; cremation is stated plainly as a place-fact, never sensational, and any belief ABOUT the river's power belongs to theology. Accuracy rail: 84 is the official ghat count; keep the source (Gaumukh/Gangotri, the Bhagirathi headstream) distinct from where the 'Ganga proper' begins (Devprayag). Dinner-test payoff: the world's-largest-delta rung — the water that dripped off a glacier ends as the Sundarbans. Lane: the river's gharials and the Ganges river dolphin are the ANIMAL bank's — keep every answer on the water, the city, and the landform.

name: Jerusalem's Old City, quarter by quarter
scope: A walled square kilometre on a ridge in the Judean hills, between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. T1: the whole Old City fits inside ~0.9 sq km of walls, split into FOUR named quarters — Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian (answer is the four-quarter division; distractors are other real gates/districts). T2: the honey-colored walls standing today were built in the 1530s–40s by the Ottoman sultan SULEIMAN the Magnificent, not by any ancient king. T3: at the city's heart is the raised platform called the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif, crowned by the golden DOME OF THE ROCK. T4: the WESTERN WALL below it is not the Temple itself but a surviving RETAINING wall of the huge platform King Herod built to enlarge the Mount. T5: a few hundred metres away, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre is shared by six Christian communities under a frozen 'Status Quo' — its front-door key has been kept by two Muslim families for centuries, and a wooden ladder on the façade has not moved in ~300 years (the 'immovable ladder'). Deep: ~11 rungs (add the Kidron Valley/Mount of Olives to the east, the Gihon Spring, the Via Dolorosa as a route).
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_City_(Jerusalem) — 0.9 km2 walled area, walls built 1535–42 by Suleiman the Magnificent, four quarters (Muslim/Christian/Jewish/Armenian), Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif with Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa, Western Wall = Herodian retaining wall, Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Immovable-ladder / Status Quo / Muslim key-holder families widely documented.
framing_note: A city sacred to three faiths at once, told as timeless GEOGRAPHY — the layout of quarters, the platform, the walls — never as current-events commentary and never taking a side on who 'should' hold it. Accuracy rail: the Western Wall is a Herodian RETAINING wall of the platform, not a wall of the Temple building itself — state that precisely. Dinner-test payoff: the immovable-ladder / two-Muslim-families-hold-the-key rung at the Holy Sepulchre. vision_mandated: name the shared and contested ground as settled geographic fact, respectful to all three.
history_overlap: Suleiman's walls (1530s–40s) and Herod's platform may echo history-bank reign/siege episodes — keep every rung anchored to the STANDING STRUCTURE and the city's present-day layout, not to a ruler's biography or a war narrative.

name: Mecca and the valley of the Hijaz
scope: A city set in a narrow, rocky valley 277 m up in the Hijaz mountains of western Arabia, ~70 km inland from the Red Sea at Jeddah. T1: unlike most great cities, Mecca grew not on a river or a coast but cupped inside a dry mountain VALLEY (the 'Hollow of Mecca'). T2: the cube-shaped Kaaba at its center is the QIBLA — the single point on Earth that every mosque's prayer-niche and every daily prayer, worldwide, is aligned to face (a geography-of-orientation wonder: hundreds of millions of sight-lines converging on one building). T3: the Kaaba stands inside the Masjid al-Haram, the LARGEST mosque in the world by area. T4: set into the Kaaba's eastern corner is the Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad) — traditionally said to have fallen from the sky and sometimes guessed to be a meteorite, though this has never been scientifically confirmed (label: legend/unverified). T5: each year the plains just outside — Arafat, Mina, Muzdalifah — host the Hajj, one of the largest recurring human gatherings on the planet, filling the desert basins with millions at once.
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca — Hejaz region, narrow valley at 277 m, ~70 km inland from Jeddah, Kaaba as qibla, Masjid al-Haram, Black Stone in the eastern corner (origin disputed, 'meteorite in legend'), Zamzam Well, Jabal al-Nour/Cave of Hira, Hajj plains of Arafat/Mina/Muzdalifah.
framing_note: Respected GEOGRAPHY, not doctrine — answers are the valley, the orientation, the mosque, the stone, the plains, never a point of belief (that is theology). Accuracy rail: the meteorite idea for the Black Stone is UNCONFIRMED — frame it as 'said to be', never as fact. Dinner-test payoff: the qibla rung — every mosque on Earth points at this one cube. vision_mandated: a living sacred site treated on its own terms, neither advertised nor dismissed; keep the same respectful register used for Jerusalem and Varanasi.

name: Uluru and Kata Tjuta
scope: A single colossal rock rising from flat desert in Australia's Red Centre. T1: Uluru stands 348 m above the plain and is 9.4 km around — a lone hump of sandstone in an otherwise flat land, the classic example of an INSELBERG (teach the term: an 'island mountain'). T2: it looks like it is on fire at dawn and dusk because its ARKOSE sandstone surface has rusted — iron in the rock oxidizing red. T3: the part you see is only the tip — the rock slab continues for kilometres UNDERGROUND, tilted nearly on end. T4: the Aṉangu are its traditional owners (the land was returned to them in 1985), and at their request the summit CLIMB was permanently closed on 26 October 2019. T5: 25 km west stands Kata Tjuta ('many heads') — 36 rounded domes of CONGLOMERATE (teach: a rock of cemented cobbles and boulders), its tallest, Mount Olga, rising 546 m, about 200 m higher than Uluru itself. Deep: ~10 rungs (add the Mutitjulu waterhole at the base, the total 863 m above sea level as a hook, the 1872 naming of Mount Olga).
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru — 348 m above plain / 863 m ASL, 9.4 km perimeter, arkose sandstone, inselberg with most bulk underground, reddish from iron oxide, Aṉangu owners (returned 26 Oct 1985), climb ban took effect 26 Oct 2019; and /Kata_Tjuta — 36 conglomerate domes, Mount Olga 1,066 m ASL / ~546 m above plain, 25 km east, name = 'many heads'.
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER: geology and custodianship, told with respect for the Aṉangu as the site's owners — never 'exotic' or 'primitive'. Accuracy rail: Uluru is arkose sandstone and Kata Tjuta is conglomerate — different rocks; teach inselberg and conglomerate before testing them. Dinner-test payoff: the underground-slab rung — the giant rock is just the visible tip. vision_mandated: the climb closed AT THE OWNERS' REQUEST — state it as their decision, plainly and respectfully. Lane: the desert's animals (thorny devil, etc.) are the ANIMAL bank's — keep answers on the rock, its color-chemistry, and the landform.

name: The Camino de Santiago
scope: The great pilgrim road across northern Spain to Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, where a cathedral holds the shrine of St James. T1: the classic route, the Camino Francés, runs about 800 km — walkers start in France at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port and cross the PYRENEES into Spain at Roncesvalles. T2: the hardest middle stretch is the MESETA — a vast, shadeless high plateau of Castile with the horizon in every direction. T3: the whole route is made findable on the ground by two humble marks — the scallop SHELL and painted YELLOW ARROWS pointing the way. T4: many walkers do not stop at the cathedral but push on to Cape FINISTERRE on the Atlantic — 'the end of the earth' to the Romans (Finis Terrae) — where the land simply runs out at the sea; medieval pilgrims said the Milky Way overhead pointed the same way. Standard: ~7 rungs (add O Cebreiro as the mountain gateway into Galicia, the cities of Burgos/León on the line).
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camino_de_Santiago — Santiago de Compostela cathedral/shrine of St James, Camino Francés from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port over the Pyrenees at Roncesvalles through Pamplona/Burgos/León (~800 km), the Castilian meseta, scallop shell + yellow-arrow waymarks, O Cebreiro into Galicia, Cape Finisterre / Finisterrae, Milky Way association.
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER: the road as a physical thing crossing real terrain (mountains, plateau, coast), told with respect — the faith that sends people walking is theology's; here the answer is the GEOGRAPHY of the route. Accuracy rail: 'Finisterre = end of the earth' is the Roman name/idea, and the scallop shell + yellow arrows are the actual modern waymarks — keep those concrete. Dinner-test payoff: the Finisterre rung — walking on past the goal until the continent ends. Lane: a Galician local dish is the COOKING bank's — keep every answer on the road and the land.

name: Summits left unclimbed out of reverence
scope: An earth-and-culture THEME spanning many named peaks: mountains humans have deliberately never stood on top of. T1: GANGKHAR PUENSUM (7,570 m) in Bhutan is the highest mountain on Earth that has NEVER been climbed — Bhutan banned mountaineering out of respect for the peaks' sanctity (hook is 'highest', answer is 'never climbed'). T2: MACHAPUCHARE ('Fish Tail', 6,993 m) in Nepal was attempted once, in 1957 — the team stopped ~50 m below the top by agreement, and no permit has been issued since. T3: even KANGCHENJUNGA (8,586 m), the world's THIRD-highest, is climbed only to a point a few steps SHORT of the true summit — a promise the 1955 first-ascent team made to Sikkim's ruler that many still keep. T4: MOUNT KAILASH is the extreme case — not merely stopped-short but never attempted at all, forbidden outright. T5: the mirror image is MOUNT FUJI (3,776 m) — a sacred cone that instead invites pilgrims UP, with summit shrines and a summer climbing season: some sacred mountains you must not touch, others you climb to worship.
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org pages Gangkhar_Puensum (7,570 m, highest unclimbed, all mountaineering banned since 2003), Machapuchare (6,993 m, 1957 Noyce expedition stopped ~50 ft short, no permits since), Kangchenjunga (8,586 m, 1955 Brown/Band stopped short by promise to the Chogyal of Sikkim), Mount_Kailash (never attempted), Mount_Fuji (3,776 m, sacred, summer summit pilgrimage/climbing season).
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER across many named peaks; the SPINE is the human choice, but every rung still names a real mountain and keys a real place-fact (height, country, the stop-short custom). Accuracy rail: distinguish 'never attempted' (Kailash; effectively Gangkhar Puensum since the ban) from 'climbed to just below the summit by tradition' (Kangchenjunga, Machapuchare) — do not blur them. Dinner-test payoff: the Kangchenjunga 'stop a few steps short and keep the promise' rung. INTRA-BANK note: the Kailash rung here must key a DIFFERENT fact (never-attempted) than the Mount Kailash ladder's four-faiths/rivers rungs. vision_mandated: treat the choice not to summit as a serious, respected decision, not a quaint superstition.

name: Monasteries in impossible places
scope: A THEME of holy houses wedded to extreme terrain (covers the Mount Athos and Mount Sinai seeds). T1: at METEORA in Greece, monasteries sit atop natural stone PILLARS up to ~400 m tall above the Thessaly plain — once reachable only by rope nets and removable ladders the monks could pull up behind them. T2: those pillars are ancient river-delta CONGLOMERATE, a ~60-million-year-old rock mass uplifted and then eroded into towers (teach: conglomerate; the landform IS the reason the site exists). T3: Bhutan's Paro Taktsang, the 'Tiger's Nest', clings to a granite CLIFF 900 m above the Paro valley floor, reached only on foot up a steep trail. T4: MOUNT ATHOS is a whole self-governing monastic PENINSULA jutting 50 km into the Aegean beneath a 2,033 m marble peak — reachable only by BOAT, and closed to women (the avaton) for about a thousand years. T5: at the foot of Mount Sinai, ST CATHERINE'S — built under Justinian in 548–565 and never once abandoned — is the world's oldest continuously inhabited Christian monastery, its library second only to the Vatican's, where the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus was found.
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org pages Meteora (sandstone/conglomerate pillars up to ~400 m, ~60 Ma uplifted delta, 24 original / 6 surviving monasteries, nets & removable ladders), Paro_Taktsang (granite cliff ~900 m above Paro valley, 3,120 m, built 1692), Mount_Athos (2,033 m peak, peninsula ~50 km into the Aegean, 20 monasteries, avaton bars women ~1,000 yrs, boat-only access), Saint_Catherine's_Monastery (built 548–565 under Justinian, oldest continuously inhabited, library second to the Vatican, Codex Sinaiticus found there).
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER: the LANDFORM each monastery is married to — pillar, cliff, peninsula, mountain foot — is the geography being tested, not the liturgy inside. Accuracy rail: Meteora's pillars are conglomerate from an old delta (teach the term); St Catherine's dates are 548–565 under Justinian. Dinner-test payoff: the Meteora nets-and-removable-ladders rung. Respect rail: state Athos's avaton (women barred ~1,000 years) plainly as a fact of the place — no editorial sneer and no endorsement.

name: Bodh Gaya's Bodhi tree and the traveling sapling
scope: The place in Bihar, India, on the bank of the Falgu (Niranjana) River, where a fig tree marks the spot of the Buddha's enlightenment. T1: the site's heart is the BODHI TREE, a sacred fig, growing beside the Vajrasana or 'Diamond Throne' that Emperor Ashoka set there around 250 BCE. T2: over it rises the MAHABODHI TEMPLE, a 55 m brick tower from the Gupta era (5th–6th century CE) — one of the oldest brick temples still standing in India. T3: the payoff — the tree growing there TODAY is not the original; it descends from a cutting carried ~2,300 years ago to ANURADHAPURA in Sri Lanka, the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi (planted ~288 BCE, the oldest human-planted tree with a KNOWN planting date). T4: when the Bodh Gaya original was later lost, a cutting of that Sri Lankan tree was brought BACK to re-found the site — the parent survives through its own child.
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodh_Gaya and /Mahabodhi_Temple — on the Falgu/Niranjana (Lilajan) River, Bodhi Tree descended from a Sri Lankan sapling, Mahabodhi Temple central tower 55 m of brick (Gupta era 5th–6th c., one of India's oldest surviving brick temples), Vajrasana/Diamond Throne set by Ashoka ~250 BCE, Anuradhapura Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi planted ~288 BCE = oldest human-planted tree with a known date, cutting later returned.
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER: the answer is the place, the temple, and the extraordinary tree-LINEAGE, never Buddhist doctrine (that is theology). Accuracy rail: the current tree is a DESCENDANT, and the Anuradhapura tree (~288 BCE) is famous as the oldest human-planted tree with a known planting date — state the lineage precisely (sapling out, cutting back). Dinner-test payoff: the traveling-sapling rung — the tree at the world's most famous enlightenment site is a grandchild of one sent to another country. Lane: the fig species' botany belongs to the ANIMAL/nature bank — keep the answer on the place and the tree's HISTORY, not its biology.

name: Holy confluences and the lowest river on Earth
scope: A THEME of sacred waters and the landforms that shape them (keys DIFFERENT facts than the Ganges ladder). T1: at PRAYAGRAJ (Allahabad) the muddy Ganges meets the clearer Yamuna at the Triveni Sangam — a confluence where the two rivers' different-colored waters flow visibly side by side before mixing (a third, the Sarasvati, is mythical — label as legend). T2: that confluence hosts the KUMBH MELA, the largest peaceful human gathering on Earth — around 660 million people came in 2025, crowds so vast the riverbank is visible from space. T3: far to the west, the JORDAN RIVER begins as snowmelt springs off Mount Hermon and runs only ~250 km — but always DOWNHILL into the deepest trench on any continent, the Jordan Rift Valley. T4: on the way it passes through the SEA OF GALILEE, the lowest FRESHWATER lake on Earth (~210 m below sea level). T5: the payoff — it ends in the DEAD SEA, about 430 m below sea level, the lowest dry land on the planet, and so salty (nearly 10x the ocean) that a bather cannot sink.
source: Grokipedia attempted (403); verified via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumbh_Mela (Prayagraj Triveni Sangam of Ganges + Yamuna + the mythical Sarasvati; ~660 million in 2025, largest peaceful gathering, visible from space) and /Jordan_River (rises from Mount Hermon springs, ~251 km, through the Sea of Galilee ~-210 m, ends at the Dead Sea; Dead Sea surface ~-430 m and dropping, hypersaline).
framing_note: PLACE→WONDER: confluences, rift valleys, and salt lakes — the answer is always the landform or the water, never a doctrine. Accuracy rail: the Sarasvati at the Sangam is MYTHICAL (label it); the Dead Sea is ~430 m below sea level and still dropping — say 'about'. Dinner-test payoff: the Dead-Sea-you-can't-sink rung. Lane: this ladder keys DIFFERENT facts than the Ganges ladder (confluence + crowd + rift + salt, not source/delta) — keep them distinct.
